text: Hinc et Damascenus in epistola ad Jordanem archimandritam de Trisagio hymno, cap. II Opp. Tom. I, pag. 483; Nov. Edit. t. II; hujus Patrolog. t. XCV, col. 27. EDIT. Ad hunc porro modum definite pronuntio, Deum per Seraphim ac per Trisagium hymnum unam in tribus hypostasibus divinitatem ac dominationem tanquam per arithmeticam quamdam declarationem Isaiæ revelasse. Cur enim non bis, aut quater, aut sexcenties vocem hanc Sanctus cecinerunt? Quid item est, cur nec bis, nec ter, aut quater, aut sexcenties, hæc verba, Dominus Sabaoth, pleni sunt cœli et terra gloria ejus, pronuntiarunt, verum vocem Sanctus ter, vocabulum autem Dominus semel duntaxat Seraphim exclamarunt? An non ut ostenderent tres quidem esse sanctas hypostases, unam vero trium dominationem, unum imperium, gloriam unam essentiamque et Deitatem?
anchorLine: tionem, atque unum in res omnes imperium regnumque sine scissione possidentes. (2*)
en: Damascene says the same in his letter to Jordan the archimandrite, On the Trisagion hymn, ch. 2 (Works vol. 1, p. 483; new edition vol. 2; this Patrology vol. 95, col. 27). Editor: In this way he defines the matter: God, through the Seraphim and through the Trisagion hymn, revealed to Isaiah one divinity and dominion in three hypostases, as by a kind of arithmetical declaration. For why did they not sing this word Holy twice, or four times, or six hundred times? And why did they not pronounce the words 'Lord Sabaoth, heaven and earth are full of his glory' neither twice nor three times nor four times nor six hundred times, but sing the word Holy three times and the name Lord only once? Was it not to show that the holy hypostases are indeed three, but the dominion one, the rule one, the glory one, and one essence and Godhead?

text: Taxatur hoc loco Petrus cognomine Γναφεύς, Fullo videlicet appellatus, secta Eutychianus, qui ter Antiochenam sedem annis 471, 476, et 485 invasit.
anchorLine: Sed profecto et Petri (3) procul absint, et Severi (4)
en: Here Peter, surnamed Gnapheus (Fuller, that is), is censured; he was of the Eutychian sect and seized the see of Antioch three times, in the years 471, 476 and 485.

text: Severus hic indigitatur ex eadem Monophysitarum secta, qui anno 512, expulso Flaviano II Antiocheno episcopo, eamdem sedem occupavit.
anchorLine: Sed profecto et Petri (3) procul absint, et Severi (4)
en: The Severus meant here is of the same Monophysite sect; in the year 512, after expelling Flavian II, bishop of Antioch, he occupied that same see.

text: Crimen corrupti per scelestum hoc additamentum hymni Trisagii in Petrum Fullonem sic rejicit Damascenus (Epist. ad Jordanem archimandr., de hymno Trisagio, cap. 5, pag. 485; Nov. Edit. t. II; hujus Patrolog. t. XCV, col. 31. EDIT.) Cnaphei hoc deliramentum est, qui ingenti tumens arrogantia, aperto, ut dicitur, capite..... ac si ipsismet Seraphim sapientior foret, ac mysteriorum intelligentior, Trisagium hymnum tanquam inelegantem pannum quemdam fullonum more expurgare peritus non est. Etenim si Trisagium hymnum de Filio solo dicamus, omnis prorsus sublata est ambiguitas, atque cum Maronitis Trisagio crucifixionem adjicimus. Verum absit, ut vel hoc labiis usurpemus..... Et reipsa eumdem Petrum Cnapheum hoc nomine sic Romanus Pontifex Felix III in epistola ad ipsum data redarguit: Ut serpens Evæ, tu ipse quoque erroris venena multitudini fidelium atque auribus infudisti: traditamque ab angelis sanctissimam laudationis formam corrupisti, inserens illi: Qui crucifixus es pro nobis.
anchorLine: Trinitatis doctrinas confuderunt (5). Nam dum et
en: Damascene thus rejects the charge of corrupting the Trisagion hymn through this wicked addition, against Peter the Fuller (Letter to Jordan the archimandrite, On the Trisagion hymn, ch. 5, p. 485; new ed. vol. 2; this Patrology vol. 95, col. 31. Editor.): This is the raving of Cnapheus, who, swollen with enormous arrogance, bareheaded as the saying goes ... as if he were wiser than the Seraphim themselves and more understanding of the mysteries, is not skilled at cleansing the Trisagion hymn like some unseemly cloth in the manner of fullers. For if we say the Trisagion hymn is about the Son alone, all ambiguity is plainly removed, and with the Maronites we add the crucifixion to the Trisagion. But far be it that we should take this on our lips ... And indeed Felix III, Roman pontiff, in a letter sent to him, rebukes this same Peter Cnapheus by name thus: As the serpent did to Eve, you yourself have also poured the poisons of error into the ears of the multitude of the faithful, and you have corrupted the most holy form of praise handed down by the angels, inserting into it: Who was crucified for us.

text: Id ipsum Petro Fulloni exprobraverat Felix Papa III (epist. 4) inquiens: Quandoque enim dicis, Trinitatem propter nos crucifixam, non Christum, et cæt. Mox autem subdit pontifex, quo se hæreticus reciperet: Quandoque autem..... venisti ad pejus..... totum hymnum ad Filium referendo. Qua de re juverit attulisse quæ adversus Severum disputat imperat. Justinianus in opusculo Adversus Monophysitas, Græce per Ang. Maium edito (VV. SS. Nov. Collect. tom. VII, pag. 311; hujus Patrologiæ t. LXXXVI col. 1103. EDIT.): Nam et hoc Severus ausus est dicere, hymnum Trisagium ad solum Filium referri, Patre et sancto Spiritu a doxologia exclusis. Hoc porro nihil est aliud quam Filium, juxta Arii furorem, a Patris sanctique Spiritus substantia sejungere, eumque inducere alterius substantiæ; aut, sin minus hoc, at perinde est ac negare, juxta Nestorii blasphemiam, Christum esse Deum unumque sanctæ Trinitatis; at idem est ac quartæ cuidam personæ, secundum illorum dementiam, hunc hymnum deferre: non pervidentes, se per id, quo honorem Filio tribuere se existimant, eumdem inhonorare, ipsumque ab adoratione, quæ Patri ac Spiritui sancto defertur, separare.
anchorLine: nem (6) perverso consilio immiscentes, crucem
en: Pope Felix III had already reproached Peter the Fuller with the same (letter 4), saying: Sometimes you say that the Trinity was crucified for us, not Christ, etc. Then the pontiff adds, by which the heretic might recover himself: Sometimes ... you have come to something worse ... by referring the whole hymn to the Son. On this it may help to cite what the emperor Justinian argues against Severus in his tract Against the Monophysites, published in Greek by Angelo Mai (Nova Collectio vol. 7, p. 311; this Patrology vol. 86, col. 1103. Editor): For Severus even dared to say that the Trisagion hymn is referred to the Son alone, the Father and the Holy Spirit being excluded from the doxology. But this is nothing other than to sunder the Son, after the madness of Arius, from the substance of the Father and the Holy Spirit and to bring in a different substance; or, failing that, it is the same as to deny, after the blasphemy of Nestorius, that Christ is God and one of the holy Trinity; or it is the same as to attribute this hymn to a fourth person, according to their madness: not seeing that through that by which they think to give honour to the Son they dishonour him, and separate him from the adoration offered to the Father and the Holy Spirit.

text: Vulg. Amen. Sophronius hic Vatic. omittit vocem Κύριε, quam retinet codex Alexandrinus, quemadmodum et editio Aldina. Hinc patet codicem a Sophronio adhibitum neque cum Alexandrino, neque cum Vaticano perpetuo cohærere.
anchorLine: consilium antiquum verum (10). Fiat (11). Quo-
en: The Vulgate has 'Amen'. Sophronius here, like the Vatican codex, omits the word Κύριε (Lord), which the Alexandrian codex retains, as does the Aldine edition. Hence it is clear that the codex Sophronius used agrees consistently neither with the Alexandrian nor with the Vatican.

text: Vaticanus codex oppositam sic præfert sententiam: Ὅτι ἔθηκας πόλεις ὀχυρὰς τοῦ μὴ πεσεῖν αὐτῶν τὰ θεμέλια· Quia posuisti civitates in tumulum; civitates munitas ut non caderent fundamenta earum. Particula tamen negativa μὴ abest etiam a Codice Alexandrino. Cæterum cum Cod. Alex. non secus ac Vaticanus ac reliquæ editiones vocem πόλεις ita repetant: Ὅτι ἔθηκας πόλεις εἰς χῶμα, πόλεις ὀχυρὰς τοῦ πεσεῖν..., subesse suspicio potest, hanc repetitionem a Codice Sophronii amanuensium vitio abfuisse.
anchorLine: ipsarum fundamenta (12); ne ædificetur in æter-
en: The Vatican codex offers the opposite sense: 'Because you have made cities fortified, so that their foundations should not fall'; Latin: 'Because you have set cities in a mound; fortified cities, that their foundations should not fall.' But the negative particle μὴ is also absent from the Alexandrian codex. Moreover, since the Alexandrian codex, like the Vatican and the other editions, repeats the word πόλεις thus: 'Because you have made cities into a heap, fortified cities, to fall...', one may suspect that this repetition was lost from Sophronius's codex through scribal error.

text: Inspice attente, quomodo sanctus Sophronius singularissimam Mariæ puritatem (καθαρότητα) accenseat nominibus, quibus ipsa et spectaculum summopere admirandum, et miraculum inenarrabile, et naturæ ornamentum, et præcelsior universis ac singulis cœlestibus ordinibus, ac demum omni creatura præstantior celebratur. At vero, quo pacto esset puritatis miraculum, si quod fœdissime singulos filios hominum deturpat, ipsam quoque deturpasset? Quo pacto angelicos ordines puritate longe excederet? Quo pacto creatura quæpiam Virgine Deipara purior excogitari non posset?
anchorLine: entuisti puritate (17), et omnium creaturarum
en: Observe closely how St Sophronius reckons the Virgin Mary's singular purity (καθαρότητα) among the names by which she is celebrated as a spectacle most worthy of wonder, an ineffable miracle, the ornament of nature, loftier than all and each of the heavenly orders, and finally more excellent than every creature. But how would she be a miracle of purity if what most foully defiles each of the sons of men had defiled her too? How would she far exceed the angelic orders in purity? How could any creature not be conceived purer than the Virgin Mother of God?

text: Quo sensu in Ecclesia acciperentur verba Gabrielis ad Virginem apud sanctum Lucam, en testis etiam sanctus Sophronius accedit. Is nempe munerum divinorum cumulus intelligendus est Mariæ collatus, ut quæcunque demum cæteris creaturis tributa noveris vel excogites, longe infra gratias, quibus nobilissime exornata fuit sancta Virgo, haberi debeant. Atqui nemo ignorat, non modo cœlestes spiritus, sed et primos humani generis parentes e divinis Creatoris manibus gratia sanctificante ornatos prodiisse. Quomodo ergo creaturarum omnium prærogativæ nobilioribus Virginis prærogativis cedunt, si ad originem quod spectat, nedum cæteris omnibus ipsa anteeat, infinito intervallo splendidior non modo sanctorum angelorum, non modo protoparentum, sed ipsius quoque diaboli et angelorum ejus ortus dicendus sit?
anchorLine: quoniam et præ omnibus creaturis (18)
en: In what sense the words of Gabriel to the Virgin in St Luke were understood in the Church, behold St Sophronius also comes as a witness. He must be understood to mean the sum of divine gifts bestowed on Mary, so that whatever you may know of, or imagine, granted to other creatures must be held far below the graces with which the holy Virgin was most nobly adorned. Yet no one is unaware that not only the heavenly spirits but also the first parents of the human race came forth adorned by sanctifying grace from the divine hands of the Creator. How then do the prerogatives of all creatures yield to the nobler prerogatives of the Virgin, if, as regards origin, she is to surpass all others, and her origin is to be called splendid by an infinite interval, not only beyond the holy angels, not only beyond the first parents, but even beyond that of the devil and his angels?

text: Rursus Sophronius inculcat, nullum in creaturis cerni gratiæ donum, quod longe nobilius in sancta Virgine non resplendeat.
anchorLine: intuens (19), summis tibi plausibus acclamo : « Ave,
en: Again Sophronius insists that no gift of grace is seen in creatures that does not shine far more nobly in the holy Virgin.

text: Manifestam hic habes sanctæ Virginis a communi cæterorum miserrimo statu sejunctionem illam, quam passim in SS. Patrum scriptis recurrentem contueri licet. Quid porro est vetus maledictio, nisi æternæ mortis sententia in omnes propter commune omnibus peccatum lata? Cum ergo sententiæ indoles postulet ut ab ea maledictione liber ille habeatur qui ad liberandos alios idoneus censetur, sua sponte hinc elucet, sanctam Deiparam a communi omnium reatu immunem hic prædicari, seu potius hanc Virginis beatitatem ut exploratam præsumi.
anchorLine: a veteri maledicto liberavit (20). Vere « benedicta tu
en: Here you have that separation of the holy Virgin from the common wretched state of all others, which can be seen recurring throughout the writings of the holy Fathers. What is the 'old curse' but the sentence of eternal death passed on all because of the sin common to all? Since the nature of the sentence requires that the one deemed fit to free others be held free of that curse, it follows of itself that the holy Mother of God is here declared immune from the common guilt, or rather that this blessedness of the Virgin is presumed as already established.

text: Nisi quis malit, vocem aliquam e Græco textu excidisse, habemus Sophronium anacolutho ac figurata locutione (zeugma appellant) utentem, non secus ac usum esse Herodotum, putaverunt grammatici in ea pericope (lib. IV, cap. 106): Ἐσθῆτα δὲ φορέουσι τῇ Σκυθικῇ ὁμοίην, γλῶσσαν δὲ ἰδίην · ubi scilicet unico verbo adjuncta cernuntur bina nomina, quorum tamen alterum eidem verbo minus apte cohærere videtur. Verumtamen par erit, ut certiori aliquo hujus figuræ exemplo posthac grammatici utantur; ut enim in var. Herod. le-
anchorLine: [audivisset (21)], sancta turbabatur anima, et sermo-
en: Unless one prefers to think that some word has dropped out of the Greek text, we have Sophronius using an anacoluthon and a figured expression (they call it zeugma), just as grammarians have thought Herodotus used in that passage (book 4, ch. 106): 'They wear clothing like the Scythian, but a language of their own'; where, that is, two nouns are seen joined to a single verb, of which the one seems to fit that verb less aptly. Yet it will be proper that grammarians henceforth use some more certain example of this figure; for as in the variant reading of Herodotus ... (continued on next page).

text: Sophronium habes suo calculo suffragantem communi SS. Patrum sententiæ, qua affirmant dignam exstitisse Mariam, quæ in Dei matrem eligeretur. Atqui notum est, id maxime ad singularissimam ejusdem puritatem spectare. Qua de re juverit hic oculis subjicere, quæ in liturgiciis Ecclesiæ Græcæ precibus legimus (Men. ad diem 12 Febr. Od. α΄): Verbum suprema Deitatis majestate fulgens (et) carnis prius expers, tu, o undequaque sancta, peperisti carne indutum. A sæculo enim tu sola, o purissima ab omni macula, propter micantes puritatis radios, et propter pulchritudinem virginitatis, et propter charismata quamlibet labeculam repellentia, digna apparuisti. (Σεσαρκωμένον. Πανάγια, τέτοκας τὸν πρὶν ἀσώματον θεαρχικὸν Λόγον· μόνη ἐξ αἰῶνος γὰρ ἀκτίσι καθαρότητος, παρθενίας τε κάλλει, καὶ πανάμωμοις χαρίσμασι πέφηνας ἀξία, πανάμωμε.) De voce autem θεαρχικόν, quæ in hoc canone recurrit, legenda sunt, quæ advertit Eustathius Thessalonicensis (Comment. in hymn. Pentecost. Damasceni, n. 82; Spicileg. Rom. tom. V, p. 245), monens eam esse vim dictionis, ut nihil sublimius dici queat: Οὐκ ἂν ὀρθῶς εἴποιμεν εἶναί τι ὑπέρτερον.
anchorLine: quoniam et digna exstitisti, quæ tantorum magnalium potireris (23), et cœleste ex te gaudium
en: Here you have Sophronius voting on his own account with the common opinion of the holy Fathers, who affirm that Mary was worthy, being chosen as mother of God. It is well known that this bears chiefly on her most singular purity. On this it may help to set before the eyes what we read in the liturgical prayers of the Greek Church (Menaion, 12 February, Ode 1): 'Word shining in the supreme majesty of the Godhead and previously without flesh, you, wholly holy one, bore him clothed in flesh. For from the age you alone, most pure, free of every stain, appeared worthy by the shining rays of purity, the beauty of virginity, and gifts that repel any blemish.' (Greek: 'All-holy, you have borne the formerly bodiless Word of the Godhead ...; for alone from eternity by untouched rays of purity, by beauty of virginity and by all-blameless gifts you have shown yourself worthy, all-blameless one.') On the word θεαρχικόν, which recurs in this canon, one should read what Eustathius of Thessalonica notes (Commentary on the Pentecost hymns of Damascene, no. 82; Spicilegium Romanum vol. 5, p. 245), warning that the force of the term is such that nothing loftier can be said: 'We could not rightly say there is anything higher.'

text: Inducitur hic Gabriel gratiam sanctæ Virgini divinitus collatam miris efferens encomiis, et per hæc ejusdem animum confirmans, ne scilicet deplorandum primæ matris Evæ lapsum sibi quoque metuat. Eam autem in rem archangelus tacite comparationem quamdam inter Mariæ atque Evæ gratiam instituit, et duplici ex capite gratiam Deiparæ tanquam præstantiorem celebrat. Ac primo quidem illud utriusque gratiæ discrimen attingit, quod ad illum sanctæ Virginis metum eximendum pressius facit, et temporariæ gratiæ protogenitricis (hæc enim a congenita sibi gratia cito excidit), stabilem Mariæ gratiam opponit, quam propterea ἀθάνατον, ἀμείωτον, σωτήριον, ἀκλόνητον, ἀσάλευτον, ἀνίκητον, atque αἴδιον appellat: quæ quidem inviete præterea ostendunt, quam vetus, quamque explorata fuerit in Ecclesia doctrina, qua traditur sanctissimam Dei Genitricem in gratia confirmatam fuisse. Deinde vero nonnulla alia interserit, quæ universim ad ejusdem gratiæ præcellentiam prædicandam spectant, uti cum eam dicit ὑπέρλαμπρον, πολύευκτον, ὑπέρφωτον. Porro facillime patet, gratiam Deiparæ haud ὑπέρλαμπρον, aut ὑπέρφωτον, aut πολύευκτον præ gratia Evæ dici posse, nisi Evæ consortem Deiparam in eo statuas, quod ad primam spectat originem. Quid enim æquiparari illi gratiæ potest, quæ efficiat, ut nunquam non charissima Deo anima exstiterit, nunquam non cœlesti illa claritate refulserit? Quænam gratia majori pretio habenda ac potiori exoptanda affectu, quam quæ impediat, ne inter prima existendi initia anima Deo invisa, diabolo mancipata, in se turpissima fuerit?
anchorLine: Deum gratiam perennitèr duraturam (24.)
en: Here Gabriel is introduced extolling with wondrous praises the grace divinely conferred on the holy Virgin, and by these words strengthening her spirit, lest she fear for herself the lamentable fall of the first mother Eve. To this end the archangel tacitly draws a comparison between the grace of Mary and that of Eve, and celebrates the Mother of God's grace as superior on two counts. First he touches on that difference between the two graces: to remove the holy Virgin's fear he puts more pointedly against the temporary grace of the first mother (for she quickly fell from the grace innate to her) the stable grace of Mary, which he therefore calls immortal, undiminished, saving, unshakable, immovable, invincible and eternal; these things moreover show how ancient and how well proven in the Church was the doctrine that the most holy Mother of God was confirmed in grace. Then he inserts several other epithets that bear generally on proclaiming the excellence of that grace, as when he calls it exceedingly bright, much-desired, exceedingly luminous. Moreover it is quite clear that the Mother of God's grace could not be called more brilliant, or more luminous, or more desired than Eve's grace unless you place the Mother of God as Eve's equal in this: as regards first origin. For what can be put on a level with that grace which brings it about that the soul was never not most dear to God and never failed to shine with that heavenly radiance? What grace should be held at greater price and desired with greater longing than that which prevents the soul, in the first beginnings of existence, from being hateful to God, enslaved to the devil, and in itself most foul?

text: Comparatio igitur a Sophronio instituta gratiam exsistentiæ coævam in Maria non minus quam in prima matre Eva, astruit, imo præsumit.
en: The comparison drawn by Sophronius therefore asserts, indeed presupposes, a grace coeval with existence in Mary no less than in the first mother Eve.
note: unnumbered closing paragraph; continues note (24) of p-0237

text: Merito quæri hic potest, quid sibi velit sanctus Sophronius, cum inquit, Virginem Mariam purificante gratia præoccupatam fuisse, seu magis ῥητῶς Virginem (utique ope gratiæ) præmundatam fuisse. Nam si generatim sermo esset de gratia humanam voluntatem præveniente, sane obvius foret sensus, atque ad illud fidei dogma proposi-tio referenda esset, quo adversus hæreticos Pelagianos ac Semipelagianos profitemur, gratiam divinam humanis meritis non rependi, sed eamdem prævenire humanum quodlibet non modo opus bonum, sed etiam desiderium, ipsumque credulitatis affectum. At enim liquido apparet sancti doctoris sententiam nullatenus huc spectare posse. Ut enim reliqua prætermittamus, quis non videat, Sophronium singularem aliquam Deiparæ prærogativam celebrare his verbis voluisse? Porro quod eo sensu quisquam Dei gratia præoccupetur, adeo singulare dici non debet, ut hæreticus audiat, quisquis affirmet, aut exstitisse unquam aut exsistere quempiam posse hominem gratia exornatum, quem hac ratione gratia non prævenerit: alioquin, ut inquit Apostolus (Rom. XI, 6), gratia jam non est gratia. Sententia igitur sancti Sophronii, ad quidpiam aliud est referenda, quod et capax sit purificationis per gratiam, quodque purificatio ipsa præ-vertere vero aliquo sensu dicatur. At vero tale aliquid evidentissime habes in ipsa humana Deiparæ natura. Purificationis enim non capax modo, sed et indiga per se in præsenti conditione, est humana natura, quippe in primo parente vitiata: tum autem etiam prævertere naturam purificatio rectissime dicitur, cum gratia purificans non jam inductam delet culpam, sed ne induci-tur antevertendo impedit. Et hunc quidem sensum ipsa Sophronii verba important. Singularis enim Virginis prærogativa in eo statuitur, quod ipsa præpurgata fuerit (προκεκάθαρται), dum cæteri Adæ filii non præpurgari, sed purgari dicuntur. At quodnam demum discrimen inter purgatum et præpurgatum reperias, nisi quod illic maculam purgatio subsequitur, ut eam auferat, hic prævenit, ne inficiat? Singulare igitur privilegium quod eo loci Sophronius de beata Dei Matre deprædicat, nullum est aliud, quam singularissima ejusdem ab originali infectione præservatio. Sed et dignissimus, qui consideretur, est totus hujus loci contextus. Sophronius enim, uti liquet, ad instar cujusdam principii, e quo deinde tot tantasque Deiparæ prærogativas deducat, præmittit illud, quod ex Evangelio constat, Mariam plenam gratia fuisse. Ac rursus horum magnalium quasi rationem postea redditurus, gratiæ plenitudinem iterum inculcat, cui subnectit immensum illum munerum divinorum cumulum, quo Deipara munera cuivis creaturæ collata infinito intervallo excedit. Palam est ergo, ex mente SS. Patrum tum in ea gratiæ plenitudine, tum in illo donorum divinorum præ omnibus excessu, et munus illud, angelis et protoparentibus commune, contineri, vi cujus gratia divina ipsi exsistendi initio coæva profitenda sit.
anchorLine: purificante gratia præoccupatus es (25);
en: One may rightly ask here what St Sophronius means when he says that the Virgin Mary was forestalled by purifying grace, or rather, expressly, that the Virgin was (by the power of grace) pre-cleansed. For if the discussion were about grace in general preceding the human will, the sense would be obvious and would refer to the dogma of faith we profess against the Pelagians and Semipelagians: that divine grace is not repaid for human merits, but precedes every human work, good deed, desire, and even the movement of belief. But it is plainly evident that the holy doctor's thought cannot look to this. To set aside the rest, who does not see that Sophronius meant by these words to celebrate some singular prerogative of the Mother of God? Moreover, that someone be forestalled by God's grace in that sense must not be called so singular that a heretic would be heard, whoever would affirm that there ever was or could be a man adorned with grace whom grace did not precede in this way: otherwise, as the Apostle says (Rom. 11:6), grace is no longer grace. The thought of St Sophronius must therefore refer to something else, which is capable of purification by grace and which purification itself may in some sense be said to forestall. And you have such a thing most evidently in the Mother of God's human nature itself. Human nature, being in the first parent vitiated, is not only capable of purification but in its present condition needs it of itself; and purification is most rightly said to forestall nature when purifying grace does not remove a guilt already incurred but prevents its being incurred by acting in advance. And Sophronius's very words import this sense. The Virgin's singular prerogative is set in this: that she was pre-purged (προκεκάθαρται), while the other sons of Adam are said not to be pre-purged but purged. And what difference between purged and pre-purged would you find, save that in the one case purification follows the stain to remove it, in the other it forestalls to prevent the stain? So the singular privilege Sophronius here proclaims of the blessed Mother of God is nothing other than her most singular preservation from original infection. But the whole context of this passage also deserves consideration. Sophronius, evidently, as a kind of principle from which he then derives so many and such great prerogatives of the Mother of God, first puts forward what is established from the Gospel: that Mary was full of grace. And again, being about to give as it were the reason for these great things, he stresses the fullness of grace once more, and adds that immense heap of divine gifts by which the Mother of God surpasses by an infinite interval the gifts conferred on any creature. It is plain, therefore, from the mind of the holy Fathers, that both in that fullness of grace and in that excess of divine gifts above all others there is contained also the gift, common to angels and first parents, by virtue of which divine grace must be professed as coeval with her very beginning of existence.

text: Si gratiæ munera Mariæ collata longissime excedunt quæcunque a Dei largitate in quoslibet dimanaverint; profecto aut absurdissime affirmandum est, originem peccato infectam sanctæ originis longe præcellere, aut verius fatendum est, Virginem Deiparam non modo æque ac protoparentes cœlestesque spiritus, in gratia creatam fuisse, sed longe nobilioribus gratiæ donis in eadem illa prima sui origine ex magnificentissima Dei liberalitate ac sapientia fuisse exornatam.
anchorLine: dimanaverint (26)
en: If the gifts of grace conferred on Mary far exceed whatever has flowed from God's bounty to anyone, then either one must most absurdly affirm that an origin infected with sin far surpasses a holy origin, or it is truer to confess that the Virgin Mother of God was not only created in grace equally with the first parents and the heavenly spirits, but was adorned at that very first origin of hers with far nobler gifts of grace from God's most magnificent liberality and wisdom.

text: Sunt et alii nonnulli e veteribus, qui cum sancto Sophronio opinati sunt Verbi incarnationem tunc perfectam fuisse, cum angelus sanctam Virginem salutans ea verba protulit: Ave, gratia plena, Dominus tecum: quod quidem Sophronius adhuc disertius infra (§ 36) affirmat, cum angelum introducit dicentem sanctæ Virgini: Jam concepisti, ex quo illud Ave protuli. De hujus opinionis pretio nihil attinet hoc loco disserere; hinc tamen ultro se rursus prodit portentosa Nicodemi monachi inscitia (vid. Præfat. ad orat. Isidori Thessalon., § 8, 9, part. I, pag. 204, 205), qui hanc Sophronii orationem plus semel allegat, et nihilominus cum aliis Græculis addit, Virginem Deiparam ab originali peccato tunc demum emundatam fuisse, cum illud impletum est, quod posterius subdidit angelus. Spiritus sanctus superveniet in te, etc. Sic mira istorum sapientia novissimum oculis nostris monstrum subjicit, Virginem jam Dei Verbo fœtam, et adhuc tamen peccato inquinatam, ac proinde Deo invisam et diabolo mancipatam!
anchorLine: ipsum cerno in te Virgine commemoratam (27). (anchor read at thumbnail resolution)
en: There are some others among the ancients who, with St Sophronius, held that the Incarnation of the Word was completed when the angel, greeting the holy Virgin, uttered the words: Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee; which Sophronius affirms more explicitly below (sect. 36), where he brings in the angel saying to the holy Virgin: You have already conceived, from the moment I spoke that Ave. There is no need to discuss the worth of this opinion here; yet from it the monstrous ignorance of the monk Nicodemus again comes forth (see Preface to the oration of Isidore of Thessalonica, sects 8, 9, part 1, pp. 204, 205), who cites this oration of Sophronius more than once and nevertheless adds, with other Graeculi, that the Virgin Mother of God was cleansed from original sin only when what the angel said afterward was fulfilled: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, etc. Thus their marvellous wisdom sets before our eyes the latest monster: a Virgin already pregnant with the Word of God and yet still stained with sin, and therefore hateful to God and enslaved to the devil!

text: Sensus est: « Quomodo vere affirmari posset, hominem aut magnum evasurum esse, aut verum Altissimi Filium appellatum iri, aut Davidis throno regnoque æterno potiturum, nisi iste, de quo hæc prædicantur, vere homo esset, et omnia, quæ sunt hominis, haberet, ac propterea nisi humanam nactus esset nativitatem, humanamque abjectionem vere assumpsisset? »
anchorLine: vel magnus fiet, vel verus Altissimi Filius vocabitur (29)?
en: The sense is: 'How could it truly be affirmed that a man would become great, or be called truly Son of the Most High, or obtain David's throne and an eternal kingdom, unless he of whom these things are predicted were truly man and had all that belongs to man, and therefore unless he had received a human birth and truly taken on human abasement?'

text: Hæc videlicet spectant ad illud Geneseos (XXVII, 36): Juste vocatum est nomen ejus Jacob; supplantavit (LXX ἐπτέρνισε) enim me en altera vice: tum ad illud Osee (XII, 3, 4): In utero supplantavit fratrem suum, et in fortitudine sua directus est cum angelo, et invaluit ad angelum, et confortatus est.
anchorLine: supplantavit hostes vestros (30), et victoriam ad-
en: These words look, namely, to Genesis 27:36: 'Rightly is his name called Jacob; for he has supplanted me this second time' (LXX ἐπτέρνισε); then to Hosea 12:3-4: 'In the womb he supplanted his brother, and in his strength he was directed with the angel, and prevailed over the angel, and was strengthened.'

text: Etiam iste Sophronii locus (vide enim, quæ alias de eadem re advertimus in not. ad § 14 Orat. Isidori Thessal. in Deiparæ Præsentationem, part. I, pag. 445) eos redarguit, qui voces ἁγνεία, ἁγνή, πάναγνος, cum sæpissime de Deipara dicantur, nunquam non coarctant ad virginalem ejusdem castitatem significandam. Dum enim Sophronius scribit, ἡ Παρθένος καὶ πάναγνος, apertissime virginalem puritatem distinguit ab τῆς ἁγνείας, et exinde elucet, eas voces latius ad omnimodam puritatem exprimendam usurpatas fuisse. Neque vero putes, id singulare Sophronio fuisse; nam (ut alia nunc missa faciam) ecce tibi eadem distinctio et in Menæis occurrit (die 10 Dec. ad Vesp.): Λαὸν τὸν ἀνομώτατον ἀδίκως καθηλοῦντά σε ἐπὶ ξύλου ἡ Παρθένος καὶ ἁγνὴ καὶ Μήτηρ σου ὁρῶσα, ὡς Συμεὼν προέφησε, τὰ σπλάγχνα, Σῶτερ, διετέτρωτο: Cum ab improbissimo populo inique te, o Salvator, clavis in ligno confixum cerneret innocens illa et Virgo et Mater tua, doloris gladio corde transfigebatur. Illud etiam adverte, quomodo SS. Patrum animis altissime defixa imago tum puritatis omnimodæ tum altissimæ præ omnibus creaturis eminentiæ, quæ refulgent in sancta Virgine, efficiat, ut hæ laudes, etiam ubi nihil tale res postulat, sponte sua e calamo fluant, ac proinde Sophronius etiam [continues on p-0243: hoc loco Deiparam et purissimam (πάναγνος) et creaturis omnibus præcellentiorem (πάσης τῆς κτίσεως προδχουσα) concelebret.]
anchorLine: plane immaculata (31), atque universis simul crea- (anchor read at thumbnail resolution)
en: Also this passage of Sophronius (for see what we have noted elsewhere on the same matter in the note to sect. 14 of the Oration of Isidore of Thessalonica on the Presentation of the Mother of God, part 1, p. 445) refutes those who, though the words hagneia, hagne, panagnos are very often said of the Mother of God, always restrict them to signifying her virginal chastity. For when Sophronius writes 'the Virgin and all-pure', he plainly distinguishes virginal purity from 'chastity', and from this it is clear that those words were used more widely to express purity of every kind. Nor should you think this peculiar to Sophronius; for (to leave other examples aside) the same distinction occurs in the Menaia (10 December, at Vespers): 'The Virgin, pure and your Mother, seeing the most lawless people unjustly nailing you to the tree, as Symeon foretold, was pierced in her inward parts, Saviour': when she, innocent, both Virgin and your Mother, beheld you, O Saviour, fixed with nails to the wood by a most wicked people, she was pierced to the heart by the sword of sorrow. Note this too: how deeply the image of purity of every kind, and of an eminence above all creatures, which shines in the holy Virgin, is fixed in the minds of the holy Fathers, so that these praises flow spontaneously from the pen even where the subject demands nothing of the kind, and therefore Sophronius also ... (continues on next page).

text: hoc loco Deiparam et purissimam (πάναγνος) et creaturis omnibus præcellentiorem (πάσης τῆς κτίσεως προύχουσα) concelebret.
anchorLine: plane immaculata (31) [p-0242]
en: ... in this place celebrates the Mother of God both as most pure (panagnos) and as more excellent than all creatures (surpassing all creation).

text: Hæc referenda sunt ad historiam quæ tradit Mariam templo oblatam, atque in ejusdem templi recessibus educatam fuisse. Luculentius id patet ex iis, quæ angelus inducitur Virgini respondens (inf. § 34). Mariæ ex voto parentum Annæ ac Joachimi templo oblatæ testem habes etiam Cosmam, cujus Commentarios in S. Gregorii Nazianzeni Carmina, Græce edidit vir Em. Angelus Mai, Spic. Rom. tom. II, part. II. (Vid. Comm. ad Carm. II, v. 423, p. 56.)
anchorLine: neque cum viris educatam (32), neque cum pueris (anchor read at thumbnail resolution)
en: This is to be referred to the story which relates that Mary was offered to the temple and brought up in the recesses of that same temple. It is shown more clearly by what the angel is brought in as answering the Virgin (below, sect. 34). For Mary's being offered to the temple by the vow of her parents Anna and Joachim you have also the witness of Cosmas, whose Commentaries on the poems of St Gregory Nazianzen were edited in Greek by the eminent Angelo Mai, Spicilegium Romanum vol. 2, part 2. (See Commentary on Poem 2, v. 423, p. 56.)
